title: College Athletics
contentHtml:
I am participating in college athletics here at SRJC, and I will be talking about the struggles and accolades that a college athlete goes through in their sport.


College athletics is hard. Your practice takes up to 3 hours 5 - 6 days a week, and games are at least 4.5 hours long (for soccer, depending on the sport it may be longer) and if you are traveling, it could be a 12 hour day.


But the effort is so rewarding. Going to Kezar Stadium (an iconic place in SF) and playing a scrappy game that you could have lost but won, eating afterwards as a team, having that brotherhood with 35+ guys ... you just don't get that often in life. There is nothing like the rush of watching your goalkeeper save a penalty kick in a situation that would have swiched the momentum of the game!


And within that reward comes more attributes that can be applied to every other aspect of life: discipline, time management, communication, hard work ethic, dedication, and learning to sacrifice.

Because you don't just magically get to play a sport at a college. You have to manage academics on top of playing/practicing and maybe working too. You have to sacrifice spending time with friends, going to a wedding in order to go to a game (one of my teammates is doing that for our Friday 9/18 game), and you may not be able to work either during the season. But by doing so, you are achieving a goal, and someone who can sacrifice the right thing for the moment is a man or woman who will be very successful at life.


It is important to be a good student as much as a good athlete because if you are planning on transferring to a 4 year, one of the first things a coach looks at is your grades! A 3.0 is minimum to move on, a 3.2 opens up some scholarship opportunities, but a 3.5 or 3.6! Even the difference between a 3.5 and a 3.6 is thousands of dollars. You have to have a good GPA to transfer on. That's why you have to be disciplined and manage your time well.


Being a student athlete requires sacrifice and buy in. A buy in of time, effort, and dedication. You may miss out on things that a regular student would be like, 'Why are you missing that?!? That would be super fun' or 'You are missing an important event for a game?' And that is fine of them to say.

They aren't going to understand the thrill of going to American River College, ending the first half tied 1-1, then absolutely smashing them to win 5-1 and having a great in-N-Out burger meal afterwards and a singing bus ride home.


Or the disappointment and anger of going to Folsom and having them score on us on a counter attack from our corner, and then the suspense of us having 3 last minute opportunities to score to only lose 0-1. Someday they might understand why we play the sport we do.


We do it because we love it, and it is rewarding on so many levels.


At the end of a day, though, it is just a game.


But for some it is life.

title: Pre-rendering
contentHtml:
Next.js has two forms of pre-rendering: **Static Generation** and **Server-side Rendering**. The difference is in **when** it generates the HTML for a page.

- **Static Generation** is the pre-rendering method that generates the HTML at **build time**. The pre-rendered HTML is then _reused_ on each request.

- **Server-side Rendering** is the pre-rendering method that generates the HTML on **each request**.

Importantly, Next.js lets you **choose** which pre-rendering form to use for each page. You can create a 'hybrid' Next.js app by using Static Generation for most pages and using Server-side Rendering for others.

title: SSG-SSR
contentHtml:
We recommend using **Static Generation** (with and without data) whenever possible because your page can be built once and served by CDN, which makes it much faster than having a server render the page on every request.

You can use Static Generation for many types of pages, including:

  • - Marketing pages
  • - Blog posts
  • - E-commerce product listings
  • - Help and documentation

You should ask yourself: 'Can I pre-render this page **ahead** of a user's request?' If the answer is yes, then you should choose Static Generation.

On the other hand, Static Generation is **not** a good idea if you cannot pre-render a page ahead of a user's request. Maybe your page shows frequently updated data, and the page content changes on every request.

In that case, you can use **Server-Side Rendering**. It will be slower, but the pre-rendered page will always be up-to-date. Or you can skip pre-rendering and use client-side JavaScript to populate data.

title: To be or not to be
contentHtml:
In life we hear many euphamisms, witty sayings, and other colloquial expressions that have just been handed down (some edited) and we just accept them with a little grain of salt.

To be or not to be. Is that really the question?

First off, what does it mean to be? There is the physical and metaphysical (or spiritual) realms, but is someone who is in a vegetative state really being? They are their physically, but their mind and personality are not present. Is that a key characteristic of 'to be'?

But then a tree or a rock are just 'being'. A rock can't think or see or move on its own. But it is still 'to be'. Then do we have classifications for different things of 'to be'? Deciding upon characteristics such as movement, growth, or what would be typically thought of as 'normal' for that object of being. Is that how we should decide what 'to be' means?

To take a controversial topic, to be a man or to be a woman meant certain physical attributes (and up until recently certain social atmospheres) and characteristics had to be meant. You couldn't 'be' a man or 'be' a woman just because you wanted to be. You had to fit the physical description. But now there are trans surgeries that can change those physical characteristics. So then where do we draw the line of man and woman (which should be a hard line)? Should it be chromosomes? Have boxes saying 'birth gender' and 'identifying gender'? Maybe growing a pair of brain cells labeled 'common sense' and following the tradition handed down to us over the centuries?

I don't know, I am not a philosophist or in the gender realm sphere, but I know what I know, and what I know is that God created Man and Woman in His image, each with their own attributes that we know of because humanity has been around to see it for thousands of years.

Maybe just existing is what it means 'to be'. Or there is some characteristics that make it a bit more grey; some that enliven 'to be' and some that emphasize 'not to be'. Either way, there has to be an agreed upon set of values that set the bar. Otherwise, there is no point in debating an philosophical question.

To be alive, or not to be alive. Is that the 'correct' question?
